## Overview {background-color="#0396A6"}

- Monte Carlo experiments: consistency of the sample mean and of OLS
- Heteroskedasticity: visual inspection, Breusch-Pagan test, robust standard errors
- Bootstrapped standard errors: the paired bootstrap

---

## Monte Carlo Experiments: Consistency {.section-divider-centered background-color="#0396A6"}

---

## From TA3 to consistency

In TA3 we **fixed** $n$ and looked at the sampling distribution of an estimator across many samples. Now we let $n$ **grow**.

::: {.callout-note title="Consistency" icon=false}
An estimator $\hat\theta_n$ is **consistent** for $\theta$ if it converges in probability to $\theta$:

$$\text{plim}_{n \to \infty}\; \hat\theta_n = \theta$$
:::

**The picture we want to see:** as $n$ grows, the sampling distribution of $\hat\theta_n$ **collapses** onto the true value $\theta$.

The Monte Carlo recipe is the same as in TA3, repeated for several sample sizes.

---

## Consistency of the sample mean: your dgp


```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def simulate_means(n, R=1000, mu=0, sigma=1):
    """Generate R samples of size n de from a Normal(mu, sigma) and return R means"""
    means = np.zeros(R)
    for r in range(R):
        sample = rng.normal(loc=mu, scale=sigma, size=n)   # a sample of size n
        means[r] = sample.mean()                           # store the mean
    return means

# example: z ~ Normal(2, 1)
mu, sigma = 2, 1
ns = [10, 100, 1_000, 10_000]
means = {n: simulate_means(n, mu=mu, sigma=sigma) for n in ns}

```

::: {.callout-warning title="Your turn" icon=false}
Propose another dgp for $z$: change `rng.uniform(0, 10, size)`, `rng.chisquare(4, size)`, `rng.poisson(3, size)` and re-run the next plot.
:::

ax.axvline(mu, color="black", ls="--", label=r"$\mu$")

Same x-axis in every panel: as $n$ grows the KDE gets **narrower and taller** around $\mu = 2$.

## Consistency of OLS: a dgp with four regressors

<div class="eq-box-wrap"><div class="eq-box">

$$y_i = 1 + 2\,x_{i2} - 1\,x_{i3} + 0.5\,x_{i4} + \varepsilon_i$$

$$x_{i2} \sim N(0,1), \qquad x_{i3} = 0.5\,x_{i2} + u_i,\;\; u_i \sim N(0,1), \qquad x_{i4} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.3)$$

$$\varepsilon_i = \frac{\chi^2_i(3) - 3}{\sqrt 6}\;\; \text{(independent of } X\text{)}$$

</div></div>

- $x_2$ and $x_3$ are **correlated**; $x_4$ is a dummy
- The error is **not normal** (skewed), but it has mean 0 and is independent of the regressors

::: {.callout-note title="Recall from lecture" icon=false}
OLS is consistent if the observations are i.i.d., $E(x_i\varepsilon_i) = 0$, and $\text{plim}\,\frac{X'X}{n}$ exists and is finite and non-singular. Normality is **not** needed.
:::

---

## Monte Carlo in code

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|3-5|6-9|10-12|13"
BETA = np.array([1, 2, -1, 0.5])

def simulate_ols(n, R=1000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    betas = np.empty((R, 4))
    for r in range(R):
        x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
        x3 = 0.5 * x2 + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
        x4 = rng.binomial(1, 0.3, n)
        eps = (rng.chisquare(3, n) - 3) / np.sqrt(6)
        X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x2, x3, x4])
        y = X @ BETA + eps
        betas[r] = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
    return betas

ns_ols = [50, 200, 1_000, 5_000]
betas_by_n = {n: simulate_ols(n) for n in ns_ols}
```

---

## OLS estimates collapse onto the true $\beta$'s

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
names = [r"$\hat\beta_2$", r"$\hat\beta_3$", r"$\hat\beta_4$"]
colors = [bse_style.TEAL, bse_style.PURPLE, bse_style.ORANGE, bse_style.TEAL_LIGHT]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.1))
for k, (ax, name) in enumerate(zip(axes, names), start=1):
    for n, color in zip(ns_ols, colors):
        sns.kdeplot(betas_by_n[n][:, k], fill=True, alpha=0.25, color=color, linewidth=2,
                    label=f"n = {n:,}", ax=ax)
    ax.axvline(BETA[k], color=bse_style.BLACK, ls="--", lw=1.2)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}   (true = {BETA[k]})")
    ax.set_xlim(BETA[k] - 0.8, BETA[k] + 0.8)
    ax.set_ylabel("Density" if k == 1 else "")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=10, loc="upper left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

For **every** estimated coeff., the KDE gets narrower and taller around the true value as $n$ grows, even though $\varepsilon$ is not normal.




## Non-spherical disturbances {.section-divider-centered background-color="#0396A6"}

---

## Spherical disturbances

The **spherical disturbances** assumption includes two assumptions on the behaviour of the disturbances:

1. **Homoskedasticity**: $\;var(\varepsilon_i \mid X) = \sigma^2$
2. **Uncorrelatedness**: $\;cov(\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j \mid X) = 0, \;\; \forall i \neq j$

<div class="eq-box-wrap"><div class="eq-box">

$$Var(\varepsilon \mid X) = \sigma^2 I_n$$

</div></div>

Now we consider the possibility of abandoning one of these assumptions, and see how estimation and inference change.

---

## 1. Heteroskedasticity

Let's start by relaxing the homoskedasticity assumption:

$$var(\varepsilon_i \mid X) = \sigma^2_i$$

The variance-covariance matrix of the disturbances is now:

$$\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_1^2 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & \sigma_2^2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \sigma_3^2 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma_n^2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

---

## House prices data

The `hprice3` dataset (Wooldridge) contains 321 house sales. We estimate:

$$
price_i = \beta_1 + \beta_2\, area_i + \beta_3\, rooms_i + \varepsilon_i
$$

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
import wooldridge as woo
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

df = woo.dataWoo("hprice3")
model = smf.ols("price ~ area + rooms", data=df).fit()
df[["price", "area", "rooms", "nbh"]].head(4)
```

---

ax.scatter(df["area"], model.resid, color=bse_style.TEAL, s=30, alpha=0.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=bse_style.PURPLE, ls="--")

ax.axhline(0, color=bse_style.PURPLE, ls="--", lw=1.5)

Does the spread of the residuals look constant as `area` grows?
:::

## 2. Testing for heteroskedasticity

::: {.callout-note title="Breusch-Pagan steps" icon=false}
1. Estimate the original model and obtain the residuals $\hat\varepsilon_i$
2. Run the auxiliary regression:
$$\hat{\varepsilon}_i^{2} = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2\, area_i + \alpha_3\, rooms_i + v_i$$
3. Test $\;H_0: \alpha_2 = \alpha_3 = 0$ (homoskedasticity) $\;$ vs. $\;H_1:$ at least one $\alpha_j \neq 0$ (heteroskedasticity)
:::




**Finite sample version**
$$
F = \frac{(\widetilde{RSSE} - \widetilde{SSE})/2}{\widetilde{SSE}/(321-3)}\underset{H_0}{\sim} F_{2,\, 321-3}
$$

**Asymptotic version**
$$
n \widetilde{R}^2 \underset{H_0}{\overset{a}{\sim}} \chi^2(2)
$$


---

## Breusch-Pagan test in Python




**By hand**: the auxiliary regression

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
df["resid2"] = model.resid ** 2
aux = smf.ols("resid2 ~ area + rooms", data=df).fit()

n = len(df)
print(f"F     = {aux.fvalue:.4f}")
print(f"p     = {aux.f_pvalue:.2e}")
print(f"n R^2 = {n * aux.rsquared:.4f}")
```


::: {.callout-warning title="Question" icon=false}
At $\alpha = 5\%$, do we reject homoskedasticity? What does that imply for the standard errors of our regression?
:::

---

## Classical SE

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
summary = model.summary(slim=True)
print(summary)

```

::: {.callout-warning title="Question" icon=false}
- How does the behaviour of the OLS estimator change under non-spherical disturbances?
- Which properties of the estimator remain and which ones are lost?
:::

---

## Robust SE

Under heteroskedasticity, $\hat\beta$ is still unbiased, but $\hat\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}$ is no longer its variance. The **robust** (White, HC1) estimator is:

<div class="eq-box-wrap"><div class="eq-box" style="padding: 8px 18px;">

$$\widehat{Var}_{HC1}(\hat\beta) = \frac{n}{n-K}\,(X'X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i^2\, x_i x_i'\Big)(X'X)^{-1}$$

</div></div>

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
model_robust = smf.ols("price ~ area + rooms", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print(model_robust.summary(slim=True).tables[1])
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Question" icon=false}
Which elements of the output change and why?
:::

---

## Bootstrapped Standard Errors {.section-divider-centered background-color="#0396A6"}

---

## The bootstrap idea

The robust SE needs a **formula**. For many estimators the formula is hard (or impossible) to derive. The **bootstrap** estimates the standard error by **resampling** the data we have.

<br>

Remember the Monte Carlo experiment from TA3: draw many samples **from the population**, compute the estimator in each, look at the spread.

<span style="color:#F28627; font-weight:600;">The problem:</span> with real data we do not know the population.

::: {.callout-tip title="The bootstrap trick" icon=false}
Treat the **observed sample** as if it were the population: draw many samples of size $n$ **with replacement** from it, compute the estimator in each, and use the sd of those estimates as the standard error.
:::

---

| | Monte Carlo | Bootstrap |
|---|---|---|
| Each replication draws from | the **population** (DGP) | the **observed sample**, with replacement |
| Requires | knowing the DGP | only the data |
| Distribution centred at | $\mu$ (or $\beta$) | $\bar x$ (or $\hat\beta$) |

| Used to | study an estimator in the lab | do inference with real data |

## Paired bootstrap SE for OLS

The same recipe works for $\hat\beta$: resample **rows** $(y_i, x_i)$ with replacement, keeping each $y_i$ together with its $x_i$ (the **paired** bootstrap).

::: columns

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-2|4-6|7-8|10-11"
B = 500
rng = np.random.default_rng(123)

boot = []
for b in range(B):
    df_b = df.sample(n=len(df), replace=True, random_state=rng)
    fit_b = smf.ols("price ~ area + rooms", data=df_b).fit()
    boot.append(fit_b.params)

boot = pd.DataFrame(boot)
boot_se = boot.std()
boot_se
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4.4))
sns.histplot(boot["area"], bins=35, stat="density", color=bse_style.PURPLE, alpha=0.6,
             edgecolor="white", ax=ax)
ax.axvline(model.params["area"], color=bse_style.BLACK, ls="--", lw=1.3,
           label=r"$\hat\beta_{area}$ (original sample)")
ax.set_xlabel(r"bootstrap estimates $\hat\beta^{*}_{area}$")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.set_title(f"B = {B}:  bootstrap SE = {boot_se['area']:.3f}")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

:::

---

## Bootstrap regression table

With the bootstrap SE we build the usual table, using normal-based inference:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
from scipy import stats

table = pd.DataFrame({"coef": model.params, "boot se": boot_se})
table["z"] = table["coef"] / table["boot se"]
table["P>|z|"] = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(table["z"].abs()))
table["[0.025"] = table["coef"] - 1.96 * table["boot se"]
table["0.975]"] = table["coef"] + 1.96 * table["boot se"]
table.round(4)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Note" icon=false}
Bootstrap SEs depend on the random draws: a different `seed` or a different $B$ gives slightly different numbers (Stata's `bootstrap, reps(500)` will not match exactly).
:::

---

## Comparing confidence intervals across SE types

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
b = model.params["area"]
ses = {
    "Classical": model.bse["area"],
    "Robust (HC1)": model_robust.bse["area"],
    "Paired bootstrap": boot_se["area"],
}
colors = [bse_style.TEAL, bse_style.ORANGE, bse_style.PURPLE]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.6))
for i, ((label, se), color) in enumerate(zip(ses.items(), colors)):
    lo, hi = b - 1.96 * se, b + 1.96 * se
    ax.plot([lo, hi], [i, i], color=color, lw=5, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.plot(b, i, "o", color=bse_style.BLACK, ms=8)
    ax.text(hi + 0.4, i, f"se = {se:.2f}   [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f}]", va="center", fontsize=12)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(ses)))
ax.set_yticklabels(ses.keys(), fontsize=13)
ax.set_xlabel(r"95% confidence interval for $\beta_{area}$")
ax.set_xlim(b - 15, b + 22)
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(ses) - 0.4)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

*Same coefficient estimate for `area`, but wider confidence intervals under robust and paired bootstrap SEs.*
